Refugee rights groups are alarmed and infuriated at the decision last month by the US president to exclude almost every other demographic. They claim the decision will continue to leave thousands of refugees stuck in dangerous situations around the globe, many of whom were already vetted and approved for entry, in favor of a very small quota dominated by Afrikaners, an Afrikaans-speaking white ethnic group descended from Dutch and French colonial settlers to South Africa. This despite low take-up of US refugee slots by Afrikaners, prompting extraordinary measures from the government to attract them even in the face of apparent lack of interest, the Guardian revealed this week, and the greatness of need in other countries. During his first and second terms, Trump has signed various executive orders and his administration made significant policy decisions to halt nearly all refugee admissions, except for white South Africans. The refugee cap determination, published on 25 September, is just the latest move in undermining legal migration while also changing the demographics of who can come into the country.

/us-news/2026/oct/17/trump-puts-new-russ.headline: Trump’s new press secretary says it’s ‘unknown’ how much she’ll deal with media
/us-news/2026/oct/17/trump-puts-new-russ.excerpt: Donald Trump’s new White House press secretary says it is “unknown” how much she will engage with the press, amid mounting questions over her legal credentials after admitting she did not pass the bar exam. In a brief interview with the Guardian, Katie Zacharia detailed the whirlwind sprint to replace her predecessor Karoline Leavitt as the US president’s chief spokesperson. Just six days after receiving a call from the White House, Zacharia stepped behind the podium for her first briefing as press secretary, in a debut that has been widely panned. Last Wednesday, 7 October, a White House official called Zacharia and asked her to travel from Los Angeles, where she lives with her family, to Washington for a meeting. (She declined to specify who made the call.) Zacharia made the trip the following day, before meeting officials on Pennsylvania Avenue on Friday. She was offered the job later that day – and accepted. “I flew home, packed two bags, said hi to my kids and husband and dogs,” Zacharia said, before returning to Washington on Sunday ahead of her first day on Monday. But her first briefing, which Zacharia said she was “asked to do” on her second day on the job, was criticized as lackluster. And she has since faced intense scrutiny over her claimed legal qualifications. After her debut briefing on Tuesday, reporters asked Zacharia to name the state where she passed the bar exam. “When I moved to China”, she replied.

/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.headline: London transfer: is it time to kill off the Heathrow Express?
/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.excerpt: If Heathrow finally builds its third runway, Londoners can expect hundreds more planes flying overhead each day. But greater congestion on the ground will be a problem too. Under Heathrow’s £33bn expansion plan, 100,000-200,000 more passengers would eventually be travelling to or from the airport each day. The most eye-catching problem has been moving part of the UK’s busiest motorway, the M25, to make space for a new 2.2-mile (3.5km) runway. A thornier one may be getting motorists out of their cars, and finding more sustainable ways for the extra passengers – and thousands of staff – to travel to and from Heathrow. Although ride-sharing, coaches and buses can play a part, scaling up rail is the clear alternative. Space on the existing line is, however, at a premium, and the Elizabeth line, built with a promise of connecting business travellers swiftly and directly from Heathrow to the City and Canary Wharf, only has limited paths. With everything up for negotiation, transport experts are asking: has the time come to kill off the Heathrow Express? The obvious airport train, as unwary visitors often find out too late, may not be the best one. The Heathrow Express, which charges a whopping £26 for a 15- to 21-minute one-way hop, was long one of the most expensive airport connections around (at least until it was overtaken by the Luton Dart).
/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.trail: With fares high and passenger numbers low, plans for a third runway could bring the train’s future into question

/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.headline: Airlines should pay for CO2 removal if Heathrow expands, say climate advisers
/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.excerpt: Heathrow airport should be allowed to expand only if airlines pay for the removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, the government’s climate advisers have said. Building a third runway and new terminals, as some in government want to do, would breach the UK’s carbon budgets and make reaching net zero by 2050 impossible, on current policies, according to the Climate Change Committee. The “only way” to manage such expansion within the UK’s climate commitments was for the aviation industry to become more efficient, use an increasing proportion of “sustainable aviation fuels” (SAF) in place of fossil fuels, and pay for the permanent removal and storage of carbon from the atmosphere. Nigel Topping, the chair of the CCC, said: “The government cannot expand Heathrow airport without requiring the aviation industry to clean up its emissions. Therefore, the government should legislate policies that require the aviation industry to fully address all of their emissions by 2050, either directly or by purchasing engineered removals. The polluter-pays principle must apply.” In a report to the government on Wednesday, the CCC found that the costs of SAF and carbon removal would probably be passed on to passengers by airlines, adding an estimated £150 to the price of a return flight to Alicante by 2050, or about £400 to the price of a flight to New York. These costs would be phased in gradually over 25 years.
/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.trail: Climate Change Committee says government cannot expand airport without requiring aviation industry to clean up its emissions

/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.headline: Heathrow expansion ‘is threat to England’s largest surviving medieval barn’
/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.excerpt: Six hundred years after it was built, England’s largest surviving medieval timber-framed barn could now be “shaken to pieces” by aircraft vibrations, campaigners warn. The public has until 1 September to submit objections to the Heathrow airport expansion, which could threaten the survival of the New Barn at Harmondsworth, considered a remarkable example of medieval architecture. The barn was built in 1426 and was bought in 2011 by English Heritage, which is staging a major conference in September. Its significance lies in its extraordinary scale, as well as the near-complete survival of its medieval structural timbers. It is nearly 60 metres long, 12 metres wide and 11 metres tall, with 13 massive oak trusses holding up the roof. It was described as a “cathedral” by the former poet laureate Sir John Betjeman, who was struck by the size and atmosphere of this magnificent structure. One of the conference speakers is Justine Bayley, English Heritage’s former archaeological scientist. She told the Guardian that the boundary of the extended airport is barely a few hundred metres from the barn, which “could be shaken to pieces by the vibrations from airplanes taking off”. The barn was built to store agricultural produce exactly 600 years ago this year. The land had been bought in 1391 by the then bishop of Winchester. Bayley said: “It’s not plus or minus 10 years or half a century. How many late medieval buildings do we know when they were built?
/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.trail: Exclusive: Campaigners warn 600-year-old New Barn at Harmondsworth could be ‘shaken to pieces’ by vibrations

/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.headline: Heathrow passengers face higher fares as airport can recover early expansion plan costs
/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.excerpt: Heathrow passengers face decades of higher fares after the regulator overrode airline objections to allow the airport to charge for planning work to build its proposed third runway. The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said it had permitted Heathrow Airport Limited (HAL) to recover early costs of up to £320m spent on developing its expansion plan since 2025. The money spent on planning will be recouped through higher charges to airlines, which are typically passed on to passengers in air fares, for about between 20 and 25 years. The CAA said that it would also allow a rival expansion scheme, Heathrow West, led by the property billionaire Surinder Arora, to claim back the £4.1m it spent on its plan in 2025 before the government announced that HAL’s proposal was its preferred option. Arora’s refund, which the CAA said was needed to promote competition, will be paid out from Heathrow’s additional charges. Current charges are about £26.22 a passenger. The CAA said its decision would increase the maximum airport charge per passenger by about 15p in 2028, rising to an estimated 30p in subsequent years. The move will fuel airline fears that construction of a third runway, which HAL estimates will cost about £33bn, will pile on charges and drive up fares. British Airways, the largest airline at Heathrow, said early cost recovery would create a risk that expansion would be “unaffordable for consumers and inconsistent with a credible benefits case”, according to a CAA document.
/environment/2026/oct/16/healey-pro-grow.trail: Civil Aviation Authority says airport can recoup £320m through higher airline charges, which are usually passed on to travellers

/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.headline: Reform UK-run council boycotts reporter after row over potholes
/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.excerpt: Rows over potholes and a viral story about a garden gate have led to Reform UK’s latest confrontation with local media, after one of its councils announced it would refuse to engage with a reporter behind the stories. Reform-run Derbyshire county council has been accused of setting a “dangerous precedent” after withdrawing all cooperation with Eddie Bisknell, a Derbyshire Live journalist who is publicly funded to cover local democracy. Stephen Reed, the Reform council’s deputy leader, said the reporter would now have to work “twice as hard” to do his job after confirming that Bisknell’s inquiries would be ignored. It comes after a neighbouring Reform council last year banned journalists from a major local newspaper. Nottinghamshire county council eventually ended its ban on the Nottingham Post and its website, Nottinghamshire Live, after being threatened with legal action. In the Derbyshire case, Reform said its decision had been made after a “prolonged period of concerns”, which culminated in a story about potholes. Councillors had hoped to produce positive headlines with a press release stating that the number of potholes in the county had been slashed from 12,000 in April to less than 700 – a figure it described as the lowest recorded in over a year. However, an article by Bisknell, one of a group of local democracy reporters funded by the BBC, reported that questions had been raised about statistics used in the release.
/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.trail: Derbyshire county council accused of ‘worst kind of double speak’ as it denies banning local democracy journalist but says it will ignore his inquiries

/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.headline: Reform UK-led council ends support for Show Racism the Red Card
/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.excerpt: Anti-racism education in some schools will be scrapped after a city council now led by Reform UK ended its 30-year support for the charity Show Racism the Red Card. Announcing the decision last week, the Reform leader of Sunderland city council, Christopher Eynon, said it would no longer support “politically charged organisations with an agenda”. Gary Bennett, the former Sunderland AFC captain and the charity’s head coach, said he was “shocked and disappointed” that Nigel Farage’s party had withdrawn vital funding. The move prompted a furious backlash from opposition politicians including Labour’s Bridget Phillipson, who described it on Tuesday as “misguided, cruel and in no way backed by the people of Sunderland”. Bennett, who became only the second black player in Sunderland’s history when he joined the club in 1984, was a founding member of Show Racism the Red Card when it was established in 1996. The former centre-back, who remains a cult hero on Wearside, said he was “surprised, shocked and disappointed” that Sunderland council – the first local authority to have supported it – was cutting its ties after 30 years. Bennett said it would immediately disrupt the charity’s ability to teach local children in schools and provide workshops in prisons and workplaces. He said: “We’re not a political charity – they’re trying to say we are but we’re not. Sunderland were the first council to come onboard to help fund us, that’s the annoying thing.
/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.trail: Charity’s head coach ‘shocked’ after Sunderland council leader says it will not support ‘politically charged’ groups

/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.headline: Reform UK activists squabble over Farage’s plan for £72m donations
/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.excerpt: For Nigel Farage, the £72m lavished last week on his party by the crypto billionaire donors Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne finally places Reform UK on a level playing field with its political rivals. The donations are the largest received by a UK political party since declarations became required in 2001 and led to warnings Farage was aiming to “buy” his way to power, with a row still raging over whether they are legal. Yet among Reform’s grassroots, the fattening of party coffers comes with challenges of its own, with some activists less than impressed by Farage’s announcement that the money would be used to hire 400 campaign managers in target constituencies. “We need more activists to knock on doors NOT managers,” one posted on a Facebook group used by Reform activists, where the sentiment was not unusual. Another party member, and former candidate, told others he was “puzzled” by Farage’s announcement, adding that the campaign managers would need an army of volunteer doorknockers. “Those campaign managers will rapidly learn that they can’t get nearly enough volunteers to do that. Are Reform planning actually to pay them too, not just the managers?” he asked. “And what happens to the ordinary branch members currently serving as campaign managers having been elected by their membership to that role?” Substantial spending by Reform on professional organisers is already under way.
/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.trail: Crypto billionaires’ £72m will be used to hire campaign managers and professional staff in target constituencies

/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.headline: London mayoral contenders limber up for a race that is Sadiq Khan’s to lose
/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.excerpt: The bicycles have been brought out and eager fists are getting ready to knock on hundreds of doors as the race for one of the most sought-after jobs in British politics springs into action. Sadiq Khan has had a vice-like grip on London, but a range of candidates hoping to unseat him in 2028 have announced themselves. The three-time mayor has been coy about whether he will stand again, and said he would make a decision next year. At the weekend, the former home secretary James Cleverly was seen riding a wobbly Lime bike through London, declaring that “London Bridge has got its mojo back” and that he has a “soft spot for Ealing”, where he met his wife, Susie. Cleverly, the MP for Braintree in Essex, has declared he will seek to be the Conservative mayoral candidate. “I’m going to run as an aspirational, entrepreneurial, forward-thinking Conservative candidate that is in tune with the city,” he said, adding that he thought he could beat Khan even though London is a left-leaning city: “London is a much more pragmatic city when it comes to voting.” Also standing in the contest to become the Tory mayoral candidate is Festus Akinbusoye, a Westminster councillor and Britain’s first ever black police commissioner. He says he is the right candidate because he is a “fresh face”, adding: “I’ve not been part of a government in the past, but I come with solid private sector experience.” But the contest appears to be Khan’s to lose, at the moment.
/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.trail: Tories and Reform hope to unseat the incumbent by tempting some Labour voters to shift to the right

/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.headline: Reform council leader, 20, defends record one year on: ‘The establishment will throw anyone under the bus’
/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.excerpt: George Finch, who made history last year after he was elected as leader of Warwickshire county council at the age of 19, is no stranger to criticism. His year at the helm of a minority Reform administration has been dominated by a string of controversies, including three code of conduct investigations and a no-confidence call – which he survived by just one vote. The latest controversy concerns a dispute over the region’s libraries. In June, Finch claimed he had received “a number” of complaints from people that the county’s libraries had been “promoting contested gender ideology”, prompting Warwickshire Pride to issue a statement, and the launch of the latest misconduct investigation. However, on Tuesday, the Labour MP Rachel Taylor accused Finch of attempting to “manufacture outrage”, citing data obtained via a freedom of information request that showed zero complaints had been made about books inappropriate for children in Warwickshire libraries since at least March 2024. In response, Finch said he had “personally spoken” to people who had raised concerns and accused the Labour MP of a “desperate attempt” to “manufacture a political argument”. It is just one of several public spats that has come to define Finch’s polarising leadership. He told the Guardian he was being targeted because of his attempts to challenge the status quo at the council.
/politics/2026/oct/16/reform-councillor-.trail: George Finch plagued by bullying claims and other controversies since taking helm at Warwickshire council
